ai.definition: Space-Based Solar Power (SBSP) involves capturing solar energy from satellites orbiting the Earth and transmitting it back to receiving stations on the ground using wireless power transmission.
ai.howItWorks: Satellite arrays collect sunlight in space where there is no atmosphere to scatter or absorb radiation, converting it into microwaves or lasers. These are then directed towards a rectenna (rectifying antenna) on the Earth's surface, which converts the energy back into electricity for distribution.
ai.problemSolved: Addressing the intermittency and limitations of ground-based solar power due to weather conditions and night-time darkness.
ai.manufacturing: Requires advanced materials and precise manufacturing techniques. The satellites need robust solar panels and heat-resistant components capable of enduring space environments.
ai.buildProcess: Involves satellite design, construction, launch, deployment, and maintenance. Each component must be carefully engineered to withstand the harsh conditions of space.
ai.costDrivers: High initial investment in satellite fabrication, launch costs, and ongoing maintenance. Energy transmission efficiency and rectenna technology also significantly impact costs.
ai.lifecycleOutlook: Potential for long-term viability but requires significant technological advancements and cost reductions before widespread implementation is feasible.
ai.regulation: Currently in a nascent stage, with no specific regulations in place. Will likely require international agreements to manage space debris and ensure safety.
ai.risks: Technological challenges, high initial costs, environmental impacts of launches, potential for interference with other satellite communications, and geopolitical tensions over resource control.
ai.profitability: Uncertain due to current lack of infrastructure and regulatory frameworks. Potential profitability in the long term if technological hurdles are overcome and demand for clean energy increases.
ai.futureDevelopment: Focus on improving solar panel efficiency, reducing launch costs through reusable rockets, enhancing energy transmission technologies, and developing sustainable materials.

glossary.def: Rectifying antenna used to convert microwave or laser energy into electricity on Earth
Waves used for transmitting solar power from space to the ground

subsystems.name: Solar collection
subsystems.role: converts sunlight to electricity in orbit, where there is no night or weather.

subsystems.name: Power conversion and transmission
subsystems.role: turns the electricity into a microwave or laser beam aimed at a ground station.

subsystems.name: Structure and thermal control
subsystems.role: holds enormous, fragile arrays together and radiates waste heat.

subsystems.name: Orbit and assembly
subsystems.role: places the satellite and builds it from launched modules.

subsystems.name: Ground segment
subsystems.role: receives the beam and feeds electricity into the grid.

buildSteps.title: Design and simulate
buildSteps.detail: Model the beam spread, orbital position and ground footprint so the power density stays safe.

buildSteps.title: Make the lightweight parts
buildSteps.detail: Fabricate radiation-hard solar cells and high-power transmitters that are as light as possible per kilowatt.

buildSteps.title: Launch modules
buildSteps.detail: Send many payloads to orbit on reusable rockets, since a full plant would mass thousands of tonnes.

buildSteps.title: Assemble in orbit
buildSteps.detail: Robots or self-deploying modules connect the arrays, transmitters and structure into one large platform.

buildSteps.title: Deploy and aim
buildSteps.detail: Unfurl the arrays, point the transmitting antenna at a dedicated ground rectenna and switch on at low power.

buildSteps.title: Test beaming
buildSteps.detail: Measure how much power arrives at the rectenna, how the beam behaves in the atmosphere and whether it can be steered off-target instantly.

buildSteps.title: Operate and maintain
buildSteps.detail: Keep station, replace failed modules and beam power to the grid, initially for short intervals.

buildSteps.title: Scale up
buildSteps.detail: Add more satellites and larger rectennas until the system delivers continuous baseload power.

prerequisites.why: reusable rockets exist, but the cost per kilogram is still far above what a gigawatt-scale plant would need.
space stations are assembled by astronauts and robots, but not yet at the scale of a kilometre-wide solar platform.
microwave and laser power beaming work in the lab and in small orbital demos, but not at megawatt scale over thousands of kilometres.
spacecraft solar panels exist, but space-based solar power needs a much higher power-to-mass ratio.
no agreed global framework exists for beaming high-power microwaves through airspace and onto land.
a receiving antenna would cover many square kilometres, requiring land, grid access and public acceptance.

pathway.milestone: small satellite experiments have demonstrated wireless power transfer in orbit
pathway.unlocks: proof that the basic beaming physics can work in space.

pathway.milestone: kilowatt-scale platforms assembled in low Earth orbit and beamed to a small rectenna
pathway.unlocks: real data on efficiency, steering and thermal behaviour.

pathway.milestone: a megawatt-scale pilot in geostationary orbit feeding a dedicated ground station
pathway.unlocks: a credible engineering and cost baseline for commercial plants.

pathway.milestone: gigawatt-scale fleets of satellites beaming to large rectennas
pathway.unlocks: firm, weather-independent power that can be exported between continents.
